paragraphs.text: Mitchell-Riley syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its features are neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, intestinal atresia (duodenal and/or jejunal), and aplasia or hypoplasia of the gallbladder. Many affected infants have died in the first year of life (Mitchell et al., 2004). Some patients with RFX6 mutations have a milder course, with diabetes beginning in childhood rather than the neonatal period, no liver disease, and longer survival (Sansbury et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Martinez-Frias et al. (1992) studied 2 sibs born to consanguineous parents. Both had a multiple congenital anomaly pattern of low birthweight, tracheoesophageal fistula, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, hypoplastic pancreas, and hypospadias. The authors considered this a previously unreported autosomal recessive syndrome. A computerized search of the Spanish Collaborative Study of Congenital Malformations (ECEMC) identified 3 other unrelated infants with intestinal atresias, hypospadias, and low birth weight. The authors suggested that these infants might represent a milder expression of the same syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (2004) reported 5 infants: 2 sib pairs from 2 families and 1 isolated case. One sib pair was born to consanguineous parents. The infants presented with neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal atresia, duodenal atresia, and gallbladder aplasia or hypoplasia. Four of the children died in the first year of life despite aggressive medical management. One patient, with a milder form, was surviving free of insulin. On pancreatic immunohistochemistry, there were a few scattered chromogranin-A-positive cell clusters but a complete absence of insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin.

paragraphs.text: Chappell et al. (2008) reported a patient born to consanguineous parents who had neonatal diabetes, intestinal atresias, and gallbladder agenesis. They proposed that previously reported cases with overlapping features, such as malrotation, biliary atresia, and pancreatic hypoplasia (e.g., those described by Martinez-Frias), may represent variations of the same syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) described infants with neonatal diabetes and small bowel obstruction due to bowel atresia. Pancreatic size was somewhat reduced, but there was no exocrine enzyme deficiency. The infants also had a hypoplastic gallbladder and intractable diarrhea that did not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement. Two cases came to autopsy, including their proband 1, a girl born to first cousins who died in the first few months of life. Both showed a normal-appearing exocrine pancreas containing clusters of chromogranin A-positive cells, but no cells staining for insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin. Of their probands with RFX6 mutations, 3 died in the first few months of life. Proband 2 was alive at 4.5 years. Proband 3 was alive at 9 years and was intermittently off insulin.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported 2 double first cousins of Turkish origin from a single family, both aged 9 years at the time of the report. The first was a girl born at 32 weeks' gestation with a birth weight of 1.65 kg (42nd centile). She had duodenal atresia, jejunal web, and Meckel diverticulum, and her gallbladder was absent. Hyperglycemia was noted at 2 years of age, and she presented with diabetic ketoacidosis at 3 years. Insulin and C-peptide levels were low, and islet autoantibodies were absent. She had gastrointestinal bleeding, and gastric heterotopia was found in the small bowel. Her liver function tests were normal. The second patient was a boy born at 34 weeks' gestation with a birth weight of 1.70 kg (7th centile). He had duodenal atresia and midgut malrotation. Asymptomatic fasting hyperglycemia was noted at 5 years, and diabetes was diagnosed at 6 years when he presented with hyperglycemia (16.0 mmol/l). He had no islet autoantibodies. His past history included chronic iron deficiency anemia. No structural abnormality of the hepatobiliary tract was identified, and his liver function tests had always been normal. Sansbury et al. (2015) also reviewed 8 previously reported cases. All had duodenal atresia, 7 of 8 had gallbladder agenesis, and 7 of 8 had intrahepatic cholestasis. Five of the 8 children had died, all within the first year of life.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) used targeted capture and deep sequencing of exons in the shared homozygous regions in proband 2, the offspring of second cousins. The only nonsynonymous novel variant they found was a homozygous ser217-to-pro (S217P) substitution in the RFX6 gene. They then sequenced RFX6 directly and identified mutations in 5 of 6 probands. Proband 1 was homozygous for loss of the splice donor site in intron 2 (IVS2+2T-C). Proband 3 was compound heterozygous for loss of the splice donor site in intron 6 (IVS6+2T-G) and disruption of the splice acceptor site in intron 1 (IVS1-12A-G). Proband 4 was homozygous for an out-of-frame deletion in exon 7. Proband 5 was homozygous for an arg181-to-gln (R181Q) substitution at a highly conserved arginine in the DNA-binding domain. All mutations were inherited from carrier parents. Homozygous severe mutations were associated with death in early infancy, whereas milder genotypes were associated with survival. In functional studies, R181Q completely abrogated DNA binding, whereas S217P only modestly reduced DNA binding and did not affect dimer formation. In autopsy pancreas from proband 1, properly spliced RFX6 transcript was not detected. The authors found no RFX6 mutation in proband 6. Because DNA from this proband was not available, they sequenced both parents and found no point mutation in RFX6 or NEUROG3, and long-range PCR showed no deletion of RFX6. They could not rule out a de novo mutation but considered this case most likely a phenocopy.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) studied 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome. Both had duodenal atresia and developed diabetes in childhood, at 3 and 6 years of age. They were compound heterozygous for 2 nonsense mutations in the RFX6 gene. One was a c.2176C-T transition in exon 17, resulting in an arg726-to-ter (R726X) substitution. The other was a c.2596C-T transition in exon 18, resulting in an arg866-to-ter (R866X) substitution. Both fathers were heterozygous for R726X, and both mothers were heterozygous for R866X. The R726X mutation is predicted to undergo nonsense-mediated decay.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) studied 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome and childhood-onset diabetes. In the RFX6 gene, they were compound heterozygous for a c.2596C-T transition in exon 18, resulting in an arg866-to-ter (R866X) substitution, and the R726X mutation. Both mothers were heterozygous for R866X. This mutation lies within 50 nucleotides of the last exon-exon boundary and is predicted to escape nonsense-mediated decay, producing a truncated protein that keeps the full DNA-binding domain. The authors suggested that partial retention of function might explain the milder phenotype and later onset of diabetes in these patients.
